f6ba9e72bab4: Tradition Four answers the oldest threat to a group: somebody outside it deciding how it should be run, and one of the first to try was A.A.'s own co-founder. Bill W. wanted to manage the whole movement from New York, and he told what happened (A.A. Comes of Age): "But I soon found that I could do no such thing. The Long Form wrote their answer down (Big Book, p. 563): "With respect to its own affairs, each A.A. group should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience." Its own affairs means its own business: when and where it meets, how the meeting runs, who serves, what the basket pays for. No other authority means none at all: not the founder, not the office in New York, not the landlord. If the man who helped start A.A. couldn't run a group from outside, nobody can. Today the outside manager is usually the building: a facility that sets the meeting's time, format and chair, and can end it when its program changes. Test it tonight: ask who decided how your meeting runs, and when the members last voted on it.

40ab7ddb3019: Before Tradition Four was written, the groups around New York had settled that no group answers to another, not even the one that started it. Bill W. told the story in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 20). The Manhattan club had nurtured the first suburban groups. As they grew they found their own rooms and their own friends. The club ran a central meeting and paid a secretary who took calls for the whole area, so, Bill admitted, New Yorkers thought "our outlying groups ought financially to support the Manhattan club; dutiful children should look after their" parents. Nary a cent means not one cent. Members gave as they chose; the groups kept their money for their own affairs, and nobody could make them do otherwise. That is the Long Form's first sentence before it was written down (Big Book, p. 563): each group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience." Today the parent may be a big meeting, an office or a program that started a group and still expects it to obey. Test it tonight: ask whether any older group, office or person can tell your group what to do with its basket.

8c2ce6d72b2c: When A.A. grew too fast to be run by anyone, the danger was that someone would try anyway, and the answer was to let each group govern itself under shared principles. By 1941 the Big Book counts 8,000 members, and its foreword asks what everyone feared (p. xviii): "Would there be quarrels over membership, leadership, and money?" It answers on the next page (p. xix): "Soon A.A. was beset by these very problems on every side and in every group." No office could have refereed thousands of group fights by mail, and nobody had the right to. So, the foreword goes on, "we had to evolve principles by which the A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole could survive and function effectively." Notice the two levels: the groups, and A.A. as a whole. That is the shape of Tradition Four. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) gives each group its own affairs, "responsible to no other authority than its own conscience," and keeps for A.A. as a whole only what touches everyone. Today the fear comes back as a demand for a referee: an office, a district or a program asked to settle a group's quarrel for it. Test it tonight: when your group has a fight, ask who it expects to settle it, and whether that someone has any right to.

That is what a group conscience looks like in practice: the members in a room, with a motion and a show of hands. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) put it in one sentence: each group is responsible "to no other authority than its own conscience." The old-timers stepping back made room for it. Today the old-timers are often replaced by staff, who never retire from the room, because the room is their job. Test it tonight: ask who your group elected to serve it, and when.

a632fbaa3f1f: Tradition Six begins by naming the three things that pull a group off its job: money, property and authority. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Problems of money, property, and authority may easily divert us from our primary spiritual aim." To divert something is to turn it off its course, and the course is the drunk who is still drinking. Bill W. admitted how close A.A. came to going the other way (A.A. Comes of Age): "At that time hospitals did not want us, so we thought we would build and operate our own." The list kept growing: teach the public, change the laws, take on every other problem too. "Yes, we did dream those dreams. How natural that was, since most alcoholics are bankrupt idealists." Every dream on that list needed buildings, budgets and someone in charge of them. Each one would have put property and authority at the center of a fellowship that worked because one drunk talked to another for nothing. They tried the hospitals, and the hospitals bogged down. Tradition Six is what they wrote down afterward. Today the dream comes back already built: a facility with beds, staff and a budget, offering to be A.A.'s hospital. Test it tonight: ask what your group owns, what it pays for, and whether any of it gets more attention than the newcomer.

306504154cdc: The A.A. name is the one thing every group owns together, and Tradition Six keeps it off buildings. The Long Form, speaking of clubs and hospitals (Big Book, p. 564): "Hence such facilities ought not to use the A.A. name." The early members had to apply it to their own places first. 474118707f4f: Tradition Six answered a threat from inside: A.A. wanting to become what the treatment industry is now. Bill W. remembered the argument over money (A.A. Comes of Age). One side said: "One alcoholic carries the message to another. Let's keep it that simple and stay out of money trouble." The other side said: "We need hospitals, paid therapists, traveling lecturers, rehabilitation centers, and heaven knows what else. It is going to take millions." And where would the millions come from? "Well, we will get it from the public, just as most other good works do." Read that list again: hospitals, paid therapists, rehabilitation centers. If that side had won, A.A. would own buildings, carry a payroll and answer to donors, and the free drunk at the door would have become a cost. The short form keeps the reason in its last words (Big Book, p. 562): "lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our primary purpose." Prestige means standing in other people's eyes. The Traditions kept the groups on the simple side and put the hospitals well outside A.A. Today the second list exists, fully built, outside A.A., and it often wants A.A.'s rooms inside it. Test it tonight: ask whether anything your group does would need more money than the basket brings in, and who would be paying for the rest.

d411b547832c: A.A.'s first case was found in a hospital A.A. never owned, and that is the pattern Tradition Six wrote down. The Big Book's foreword tells it (p. xvii): "Hence the two men set to work almost frantically upon alcoholics arriving in the ward of the Akron City Hospital." The two men were Bill W. and Dr. Bob. They didn't run the ward; they walked in and talked to drunks. Bill W. named friends in medicine (A.A. Comes of Age): "Here great friends like Dr. Silkworth and Sister Ignatia came to our aid." Doctors and nurses treated the body, members carried the message, and nobody's name went on anybody else's door. Bill put the rule in one line: "Certain that we can do together what we cannot do separately, we shall always co-operate but never compete." To compete would have meant A.A. opening hospitals of its own. To affiliate would have meant A.A. becoming part of theirs. The Long Form allows the middle and nothing more (Big Book, p. 564): a group "may cooperate with anyone." Cooperation is visiting, carrying the message where the drunks are, and staying a guest. Today it often runs backward: the facility runs the room and calls it A.A. Test it tonight: ask whether your group goes into places as a guest carrying the message, or sits in them as part of the program.

9a8e8b0e8076: The last sentence of Tradition Six's Long Form is the shortest, and it usually gets broken with a signature. The Big Book (p. 564): "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one." To bind is to tie, or to put yourself under an obligation someone can hold you to. No one means no one: not the facility, the court, the funder, or the kind people who mean well. Read it as a rule about promises. A group may carry the message into a hospital or a jail as a guest. It may not promise anyone a meeting as part of their program, a weekly slot their clients are counted at, an attendance record it will keep for them, or a chair it will fill on their schedule. The moment a group owes a meeting to someone, that someone can call in the debt. Today the binding comes as paperwork: an agreement to provide an A.A. meeting for a program's clients, a form signed to keep a room, a promise to report who came. None of them looks like giving up the group's freedom. Each one is. A group bound to no one can say no tomorrow without asking leave. Test it tonight: ask whether your group has signed, promised or agreed to anything with anyone outside it, and what they could demand because of it.

16ac8c3b3483: A group can break Tradition Six out of gratitude, in one vote, with nobody meaning harm. The group has eleven hundred dollars more than it needs for rent and literature. The detox across town, where half the members first dried out, is short of money. Someone moves to give it the surplus, and the motion passes to applause. Two months later the detox's fundraising letter goes out, with the group listed among its supporters under its A.A. name. Nobody asked for that; it was the detox saying thank you. It financed the detox, and the thank-you lent the group's name and turned it into an endorsement. Every drinker who reads that letter learns that A.A. backs that detox, and may decide A.A. is the detox. A group that pays for a facility has tied itself to it, and the drunk can no longer tell the two apart. Members can give what they like out of their own pockets. The basket was given to carry the message. Test it tonight: ask where your group's extra money goes, and whether anyone outside A.A. has ever thanked your group by name.

ae961f6a0b47: The Long Form says whoever pays for a facility runs the facility, and capture is when they start running the group too. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 564): "Their management should be the sole responsibility of those people who financially support them." Sole means only. Those who pay for a club or hospital manage it, and nothing else. Bill W. watched the line crossed both ways at the early clubs (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 20): "if an A.A. rotating committee tries to boss the club corporation or if the corporation tries to run the A.A. affairs of those groups who may meet at the club, there is difficulty at once." A rotating committee is the group's elected servants, changed often so nobody stays in charge. His cure: "If an A.A. group wishes to use a given club, let them pay rent or split the meeting take with the club management." The meeting take is the basket. Rent keeps the two apart. The group is a tenant, not a department. Today the facility often pays for everything, asks no rent, and in return picks the chair, sets the format and decides who may come in. That is the payer managing an A.A. group, which the Long Form never allowed. Test it tonight: ask who pays for the room your group meets in, and what that payer gets to decide.

9215df62af78: Put the A.A. name on a fund drive for a good cause, and you have handed it to every promoter in town. In the 1940s some groups, desperate for hospital beds, started public campaigns to raise money for "A.A. hospitals" of their own. Bill W. wrote what followed (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 16): "Instantly all sorts of doubts are generated; the projects bog down. Conservative A.A.s realize that business ventures or solicitations carrying the A.A. endorsement are truly dangerous to us all. Were this practice to become general the lid would be off. Promoters, A.A. and otherwise, would have a field day." A promoter is someone who sells a scheme to the public. The beds were badly needed. The danger was the name on the appeal. So the Long Form moved hospitals out of the groups' hands (Big Book, p. 564): "Secondary aids to A.A., such as clubs or hospitals which require much property or administration, ought to be incorporated". Incorporated means set up as a separate body with its own owners. The group carries the message; the bed belongs to someone else. 333e93829b6b: Before there was a Tradition Six, the Big Book already showed a hospital and A.A. working side by side without belonging to each other. cc372234e340: A group that houses newcomers has gone into business, and the business soon decides who gets helped. Picture a group moved by the men sleeping in cars outside its meeting. 921f81450ede: Authority in A.A. grew wherever property did, and the first clubs found that out before any Tradition was written. Bill W. remembered those years with affection and honesty (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 18): "Growth brought headaches; growing pains, we call them now. How serious they seemed then!" A building needs someone to hold the keys, collect the rent and make the rules. Some ran the place like dictators. Drunks fell on the floor or broke up meetings. Steering committees, small groups set up to run things, tried to name their own friends to follow them, and found "to their dismay that even sober drunks couldn't be" steered. Nobody in A.A. has the power to govern anyone, and the property kept tempting people to try. What they worked out was to take the building's business away from the groups, so that whoever wanted the club could run it and the groups could stay what they were. The Long Form set that down in 1946 for every club and hospital: managed apart, by those who pay for it. Today the same pull works wherever one person holds the keys, the bank account or the meeting list, and the group starts asking his permission. Test it tonight: ask who holds the keys and the bank card for your meeting, and how the group would take them back.

6a1789e01355: A letter of support is how a program asks a group to vouch for it, and A.A. has already answered. Bill W. put it in one line in 1955 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 50): "We will cooperate with practically everybody, yet we decline to marry our Society to anyone." To cooperate is to work alongside: carry the message into a detox when asked, leave literature, answer the phone. To marry is to take on someone's name, terms and future as your own. The Long Form draws the same line from the group's side. Cooperation may go a long way, but never as far as affiliation or endorsement. Affiliation means belonging to someone; endorsement means vouching for them. Today the request comes as paperwork. A program applying for public money asks the local groups for a letter saying they support its work. Another wants a line for its website saying the groups recommend it. Each request is polite, each cause sounds good, and each one puts the group's name behind somebody else's business, where the drunk still drinking will read it and assume A.A. sent it. A group that signs has spoken for a program it does not run and cannot stop. Test it tonight: if a program asked your group for a letter of support tomorrow, who would answer, and what would they say?

bfb3affa5438: A group can endorse something without ever voting to, just by letting it sit on the literature table. ac39e11a0e2c: Read the cooperation sentence of Tradition Six slowly, because the rumour about it leaves out its second half. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 564): "While an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied." Take it word by word. May cooperate: a group is allowed to work alongside others, not ordered to. Affiliation means being attached as a part or a member, the way a branch belongs to a company. Endorsement means putting your name behind someone and telling the public they are good. Actual or implied means it counts whether anyone signed anything or not. If a stranger walking in would fairly think the group belongs to the place, or vouches for it, the line has been crossed. The rumour says the Traditions encourage partnership with treatment, and it quotes only the first eight words. The sentence ends with a fence. Today the implied kind is the common one: a meeting printed on a facility's weekly program, the facility's logo on the group's flyer, staff calling it their A.A. meeting. Nobody signed a contract. The newcomer still learns that A.A. is part of the place that bills him. Test it tonight: look at your group's meeting listing and flyer, and ask what a stranger would think your group belongs to.

5d8fe37b129c: Every capture this month has worked the same way: something outside the group gets a hold on it, through money, property or authority, until the group can no longer walk away. The Big Book introduces the Traditions as answers to two questions, and the second is this (Big Book, p. 561): "How can A.A. best stay whole and so survive?" Tradition Six answers it for a group's possessions and its friends. Hospitals and clubs are kept outside. The A.A. name stays off them. Cooperation stops short of a marriage. Under it all sits the last sentence: a group can "bind itself to no one." To bind is to tie, and the ties come dressed as help: a free room, a steady flow of clients, a grant, a partnership, a debt of gratitude. A group bound to no one can leave any room, refuse any money and turn down any partner, and still be an A.A. group the next morning. That keeps the door open to the drunk still out there, free. The same page says why: "We alcoholics see that we must work together and hang together, else most of us will finally die alone." Test it tonight: ask three questions. Who could close your meeting? Who pays for it? Who decides what happens in it? In an A.A. group the answers are the members, the members, and the members.

6c54714e8d47: A group that starts paying for members' treatment has gone into business, and the business soon starts choosing among drunks. A newcomer can't afford a detox bed, so the group passes a second basket and covers it. It works once. By spring there is a fund, a treasurer for it, and business meetings that run an hour over arguing whose bill to pay. One man paid his back and two didn't. Somebody asks whether a man on his third slip should get it again. Bill W. saw it across the groups (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 15): "practically all group schemes to finance or guarantee hospital bills for fellow members have failed also. Not only do many such loans go unpaid, there is always the controversial question in the group as to which prospects deserve them in the first place." A prospect is a drunk who might join. A room open to any drunk is now sorting drunks by who is worth the money. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 564): "An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business." Lending money is a business, and so is buying beds. A member's own wallet is his affair; the group's treasury is for the message. Test it tonight: ask what your group's money paid for this year, and whether any of it was a judgment on a person.

955f42e5d271: The Long Form makes the groups the ones who can walk away from a facility, and capture is when that gets turned around. Clubs and hospitals, it says (Big Book, p. 564), "ought to be incorporated and so set apart that, if necessary, they can be freely discarded by the groups." The Long Form calls them secondary aids: second in line, a help to A.A. and never part of it. Freely discarded means the groups can drop them without losing anything they need. Bill W. explained why that keeps them honest. Nobody is forced to pay for them, so (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 29) "they can never dictate, nor can they stray from the main body of A.A. tradition for very long." To dictate is to give orders. Now watch it run backward. A facility offers a group its room for free, coffee included. Two years on, the group has no treasury, no other room, and a facility rule about who may attend. The group can no longer discard the facility. The facility can discard the group, and the group knows it, so it doesn't argue. Nobody captured it by force. Comfort did it, one free month at a time. Test it tonight: if the place your group meets told it to leave tomorrow, ask whether the group would still meet next week, and who would decide where.
3814596c7ed2: The Long Form gives the groups the power to drop any facility, and a free room can quietly take that power away. Could my group walk away from the place it meets?

6b4768337d11: In 1947 the danger to Tradition Six walked in as an enthusiast with a good cause, asking for A.A.'s name. Bill W. described him (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 24): "He strongly feels that A.A. ought to place its name and financial credit squarely behind any first-rate research, hospital or educational project." Financial credit is the trust that lets you borrow or raise money. "Seeing that A.A. now makes the headlines, he argues that we should freely loan out our huge goodwill." Goodwill is the public's trust in a name. Bill named a motive without pretending it was everyone's: "The judgment of this enthusiast is sometimes beclouded by the fact he wants to make a career." Beclouded means fogged. The A.A. name belongs to every group at once, built by drunks who never charged a cent, and he wanted to lend it out. That is why the short form says a group must never lend the A.A. name to any outside enterprise, and the Long Form keeps even A.A.'s own clubs and hospitals from using it. Today the enthusiast is often a member who works in the field and asks his home group to put its name on his program's open house or its brochure. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone has asked your group to put its name to their work, and what the group answered.

6c82f89c086d: Before Tradition Six was settled, some groups ran drying-out places themselves, and Bill W. reported how it went. In those years cheap hospital beds for drunks were hard to find. He wrote in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 15): "This urgency has tempted some A.A. groups to set up drying-out places of their own, hiring A.A. managers, nurses, and securing the services of a visiting physician. Where this has been done under the direct auspices of an A.A. group it has almost always backfired. It has put the group into business, a kind of business about which few A.A.s know anything at all." Under the direct auspices means run by the group itself, in its own name. Backfired means it blew up on them. Drunks who knew how to carry a message were suddenly hiring nurses, chasing bills and fighting over who was in charge, and the message got whatever time was left. The Long Form, first printed in 1946, had already drawn the line (Big Book, p. 564): "But hospitals, as well as other places of recuperation, ought to be well outside A.A.—and medically supervised." Places of recuperation are where people dry out and get their strength back. Today the pull runs the other way: facilities want groups inside them. Test it tonight: ask whether your group runs, staffs or answers for any place where drunks are treated.

cc9e4ce0ceaa: A.A. is not a treatment, and the Long Form says so by putting treatment outside it. The rumour today is that meetings are a kind of therapy, one more service a program counts in its hours. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 564) puts hospitals and places of recuperation "well outside A.A." and adds "medically supervised." Medically supervised means a doctor is responsible, not a drunk with a few years sober. Bill W. was plain about the division (A.A. Comes of Age): "We know that theology is for clergymen and that the practice of medicine and psychiatry is for doctors." Theology is the study of God, the clergy's work. Doctoring the very sick, Bill wrote, was "not and could not be A.A.'s business." A.A.'s business is one drunk carrying a message to another, free. The Big Book lists what the member's job takes (p. 97): "innumerable trips to police courts, sanitariums, hospitals, jails and asylums." The doctor treats the drunk; the member makes the trip to see him. Neither becomes the other. Today the line blurs from the treatment side: a client's meeting attendance logged as treatment, staff chairing the meeting as part of a shift. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone in your room has been told the meeting is part of their treatment, and who told them.

83fba41dd9b8: A group goes into business one good idea at a time, and nobody ever votes for the moment it stops being a group. It starts with a literature table. Then medallions, mugs and shirts with the group's name, because they sell. The anniversary dance needs tickets, a hall deposit and a DJ, and it makes money, so next year there are two. Somebody has to keep the stock, chase the deposits and do the books. The business meeting that used to ask who would go out on the next call now spends forty minutes on inventory and ten on the drunk. Every item passed by a fair vote. Bill W. wrote in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 29): "More and more, the A.A. groups are realizing that they are spiritual entities, not business organizations." An entity is a thing that exists in its own right. A group is one with a single job, and the job isn't retail. Literature carries the message, so the table isn't the problem. The problem is a group that needs its sales to pay its rent, because then the sales come first. The Long Form says flatly that a group should never go into business. Test it tonight: at your group's next business meeting, count the minutes spent on money and stock, and on the drinker still out there.

d4cdbe0caeb9: Tradition Five gives every A.A. group one job, and the threat it answers is a fellowship trying to do everything. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Each Alcoholics Anonymous group ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." An entity is a body that acts as one. One purpose, not five. And the alcoholic who still suffers is the one still drinking tonight, not the member already in a chair. 92bd7ab727f4: "Spiritual entity" in Tradition Five says what a group must not become, and the rumour has turned it into a mood. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Each Alcoholics Anonymous group ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose". An entity is a body that acts as one. The rumour hears the word spiritual and thinks of soft voices, candles and a certain way of talking. That reading is about the feelings of the people in the room, and it lets a group feel spiritual while it is run like anything at all. Bill W. wrote down what the word was guarding against in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 32): "an A.A. group is a spiritual entity, not a business concern." A business concern is a company. So a group is a spiritual entity in the Long Form's sense when it has nothing to sell, no client to bill and no payroll to protect. Then its one purpose, the drinker still out there, has nothing competing with it. Today the rumour lets a room with a price tag behind it call itself spiritual because the talk sounds that way. Nobody's private beliefs decide the question. The books do. Test it tonight: set aside how your meeting sounds, and ask whether anyone makes money because it exists.

e439cd591352: A group can drift off its one purpose one motion at a time, and every motion can sound reasonable. The business meeting is where a group decides how it will carry the message, and that is exactly where the drift starts. A motion for an anniversary dinner. A motion for group shirts. A motion for a speaker night, then a committee to plan it, then a fund for the hall. An hour goes by. Nobody mentions the detox ward across town that hasn't seen an A.A. member in a year, or the outreach list that hasn't been updated. Bill W. learned this lesson when groups tried to run their own drying-out places, and wrote (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 15): "We have been obliged to see that an A.A. group is primarily a spiritual entity; that, as a group the less business it has to transact, the better." To transact business is to carry it out. None of those motions is wicked. Each one takes a piece of the group's time, money and attention, and the Long Form gives a group "but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (Big Book, p. 563). Business crowds the purpose out quietly, because it always feels urgent. Test it tonight: at your next business meeting, time how long the group spends on anything that reaches a drinker.
